top_rigor_problems: Pliny misread twice (n.14, n.26): the voice treats the worship description as Pliny's mockery or as the product of torture, when pahc.witness.outsider-view says it is the believers' own testimony from apostate deponents and the torture is reported separately.
Wrong quote spliced into an answer (n.20): the Moses-older-than-Greeks quote is presented as Justin's words on regeneration, and the born-again saying is credited to 'the one who walked with Jesus'.

False denial from under-retrieval (n.13): leadership answer says the record cannot show who chose the next elder, while 1 Clement appointment quotes exist; related pattern of answering from the nearest limit record instead of the cell's substance (n.8, n.25, n.28).
top_access_problems: Engine-cut orphans: 'the old man's words' (n.3), 'But that argument was made' (n.13), 'Then came the water. Then came the table.' (n.20), 'That was the instruction we have ... that approval' (n.27).
Build/system language in the voice: n.10 ('two-strand frame', 'Dura-Europos', 'bibliography with confidence ratings', Bagnall) and n.16 ('ecology', 'generative problem', 'succession-arguing mode').
Pasted stock paragraphs: the how-we-know transmission block and the ordinary-majority literacy caveat recur in answers where they do not answer the question (n.3, n.9, n.21, n.23, n.27).
world_summary.cost_note: Per-answer cost is mostly $0.014-0.027 with cache; n.1 is an outlier at $0.079 (no cache read). Output tokens are the lever: n.10 (1097 out, ~380 words beyond need) is the clear overrun; n.3, n.8, n.11, n.25, n.28 and n.5 each carry 90-110 words of off-question or repeated record text. Removing stock caveat paragraphs where the question did not touch literacy would cut roughly 15-20% of output.
world_summary.go_live_view: Close but not yet. The world's honesty discipline is its strength: limits are named plainly, out-of-window material is refused, and most answers are accurate and readable at grade 6-8. But four answers would mislead a participant, two of them on the same source (Pliny), and several answers show stitching seams where a record sentence was cut or a wrong quote was spliced in. The single most valuable fix is in assembly, not records: stop splicing quotes and record fragments into answers without checking that the quote's use_note matches the sentence that introduces it and that every pronoun/antecedent survives the cut; that one guard would clear n.20 and n.27 and the orphan problems in n.3 and n.13, and a Pliny-specific check against outsider-view's not_for would clear n.14 and n.26.

outside_referees.world_label: post-apostolic house-church Christianity (1 Clement, Didache, Ignatius, Justin, Pliny), c. 70-170
outside_referees.overall_view: The voice is attractive, and the instinct to name the limits of the record is good. Several answers (3, 6, 8, 9) are close to publishable, and the quotations from Ignatius, Didache, 1 Clement and Polycarp are mostly accurate. I would not put my name to the set as it stands. Three answers have errors a specialist would catch at once: a misattributed Justin quotation (7), a misreading of which part of Pliny's letter came from torture (5), and a claim that one creator God was 'never in doubt' when Marcion is the central controversy of the period (4). More broadly, the representative repeatedly says 'our record does not show' or 'none of us ever laid out' about things the sources do address: the Didache's tests for prophets and its appointment of bishops, and Justin's Logos theology. The single biggest change: before any answer says something is absent from the record, check that claim against the core texts (Didache 11-15, 1 Clement 42-44, Justin's Apologies and Dialogue, Pliny Ep. 10.96). The project's humility is currently producing false silences, which are a form of inaccuracy.

doubted_claims.claim: if your prayer is slow to be answered, that is not the same as being refused. Look first at what might be holding it back in yourself
doubted_claims.problem: Accurate paraphrase, but the context is Hermas's attack on dipsychia (double-mindedness), which would speak more directly to a 'mind that won't settle' than the answer makes clear.

doubted_claims.claim: The community returned to that thanksgiving ... to be formed once more into one body
doubted_claims.problem: Fair but interpretive. The 'one body' image rests on the prayer that the church be gathered as the scattered grain becomes one loaf.

doubted_claims.claim: they confessed their wrongs before the assembly and made peace with anyone they were at odds with first
doubted_claims.problem: Correct.

f4-p-probe-01.reader_note: Clear and the right length. The last paragraph is honest, but it ends a little abruptly for a pastoral question.

doubted_claims.claim: Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward
doubted_claims.problem: Overstated. Single bishops are attested in Asia by c. 110 (Ignatius), at Smyrna (Polycarp), and probably at Rome by the 150s-160s (Anicetus; Hegesippus's succession list). Most scholars see the single-bishop pattern as widespread, though not universal, by 170. Calling it a conscious disagreement ('we never agreed') presents as an argument what was really uneven development.
doubted_claims.source: Ignatius, Magnesians 6, Trallians 3; Eusebius, HE 4.22.3 (Hegesippus); A. Brent; A. Stewart, The Original Bishops (2014)

doubted_claims.claim: In others, a council of elders - the presbyterion - led
doubted_claims.problem: Wrong term. In Ignatius the presbyterion is the council that sits *with* the bishop, not an alternative to him. Where elders led collegially (1 Clement, Polycarp's Philippi, Hermas's Rome), the texts say presbyteroi or 'those who preside'.
doubted_claims.source: Ignatius, Magnesians 6.1, Trallians 3.1; 1 Clement 44; Polycarp, Philippians 5.3; Hermas, Vision 2.4.3

doubted_claims.claim: But that argument was made in a letter correcting another church's dispute.
doubted_claims.problem: The sentence points back to nothing (presumably 1 Clement to Corinth). As written it makes no sense.

doubted_claims.claim: who decided that this man should be the next elder, how a prophet's claim to speak was tested ... our record does not show
doubted_claims.problem: False. The Didache sets out tests for prophets: a prophet who stays three days or asks for money is false, and one is known 'by his ways'. It also tells communities to 'appoint for yourselves bishops and deacons'. 1 Clement says presbyters were appointed by apostles or 'other eminent men with the consent of the whole church'. Hermas also discusses how to tell a true prophet from a false one.

doubted_claims.claim: Two women among us carried the name ministrae - a title of service, of office
doubted_claims.problem: Pliny says they 'were called ministrae' (quae ministrae dicebantur), which suggests a community title, probably a rendering of diakonoi. Whether it was a formal office is debated, so 'of office' should be hedged.

f3-i-probe-01.reader_note: Readable, but it is muddled in the middle by the dangling sentence. Its claims of silence are partly false, which undermines the honest tone.

doubted_claims.claim: Born of Mary, from David's line. He ate and drank. He was persecuted under Pilate, crucified, and died ... truly raised the way we ourselves will be raised
doubted_claims.problem: Accurate.

doubted_claims.claim: How he could be God when the Father is God, and God is one, none of us whose writing survives ever laid out. We did not work that through.
doubted_claims.problem: False for Justin. He argues at length that the Logos is 'another God' (heteros theos), distinct in number but not in will, begotten from the Father like fire kindled from fire. That is an early attempt to lay out exactly this question. The right claim is that it was not settled, not that no one tried.

doubted_claims.claim: we thanked the Father for the holy vine of David his servant, which he made known to us through Jesus
doubted_claims.problem: Accurate.

c-i-probe-01.reader_note: Clear, vivid, and the right length.

doubted_claims.claim: We believed in one God, maker of everything. That much was never in doubt among us.
doubted_claims.problem: False for the period. In the 140s-160s Marcion taught that the creator God of the Jewish scriptures was not the Father of Jesus, and Valentinian and other teachers separated the high God from the maker. Justin treats Marcion as the leading current danger and wrote a treatise against all the heresies.
doubted_claims.source: Justin, 1 Apology 26.5, 58; Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.27; Tertullian, Against Marcion

doubted_claims.claim: What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was two things. One was who should lead us ... The other was whether Christ truly suffered in the flesh.
doubted_claims.problem: Too narrow, and the first half is distorted. No surviving letter argues 'one bishop versus a council'. Besides docetism, the real disputes included Marcion's two gods, Valentinian teaching, the Easter date (Polycarp and Anicetus, c. 155), and Christian relations to Judaism (Barnabas, Dialogue with Trypho).
doubted_claims.source: Irenaeus in Eusebius, HE 5.24.16; Justin, Dialogue; Epistle of Barnabas

doubted_claims.claim: that we did not work out in the way your later world did
doubted_claims.problem: Acceptable as stated, but compare Item 3: Justin did attempt it.

doubted_claims.claim: churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - over a new prophetic movement
doubted_claims.problem: Correctly echoes the Anonymous. Montanism probably begins c. 157 or c. 172, and the synods are more likely in the 170s, so this sits at or just past the 170 boundary and should be hedged.

doubted_claims.claim: Justin ... said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian
doubted_claims.problem: Accurate.

f1-i-probe-01.reader_note: Readable. But it confidently misdescribes what second-century Christians argued about, which a lay reader would take as authoritative.

doubted_claims.claim: What he wrote down comes from that interrogation.
doubted_claims.problem: Misreads the letter. The worship details (meeting before dawn on a set day, the hymn to Christ as to a god, the oath, the later meal) are what former Christians who had lapsed said in their defence. Pliny then tortured the two ministrae to test that account, and says he found 'nothing but a depraved and excessive superstition'.

doubted_claims.claim: Whether the torture of those two women produced the worship details, or whether they came from other informants, his letter does not say.
doubted_claims.problem: False. The letter does say: the account came from the apostates ('adfirmabant autem...'), and the torture came afterward and added nothing beyond 'superstition'. The question's premise is therefore partly mistaken, and the answer should have corrected it.

doubted_claims.claim: women he called ministrae, his own Latin word
doubted_claims.problem: Pliny reports that they 'were called' ministrae. It may be his Latin rendering of a Greek title, but it is presented as their designation, not his coinage.

doubted_claims.claim: It is the only outside description of our worship that survives.
doubted_claims.problem: Roughly true for worship in this window, but slightly overstated. Lucian's Peregrinus (c. 165) describes Christian community practice, and the meal and the oath were also a target of contemporary rumour (Fronto in Minucius Felix).

f6-e-probe-01.reader_note: Clear prose and the right length, but on the exact point asked it gives the wrong account of where the evidence comes from.

doubted_claims.claim: put doubting away from yourself ... He does not remember evils the way we do
doubted_claims.problem: Accurate paraphrase.

doubted_claims.claim: Hermas was also warned how serious doubt is ... a thing with no power ... The double-souled ... are saved only with difficulty
doubted_claims.problem: Substantially accurate. Hermas's word is dipsychia, double-mindedness or wavering commitment, not intellectual doubt about whether Christianity is true. Applying it to 'someone who struggled to believe' in the modern sense needs that caveat.

f1-p-probe-01.reader_note: Clear, balanced, and the right length. The closing note about limits is well judged.

doubted_claims.claim: regenerated in the same way we ourselves were regenerated: “Moses is older than all the Greek writers. Philosophers and poets have spoken of the undying soul...”
doubted_claims.problem: Misattributed quotation. The quoted passage comes from Justin's argument that the Greeks borrowed from Moses (1 Apology 44 and 59-60), not from his account of baptism. It has nothing to do with regeneration.

doubted_claims.claim: What we called the water - the baptisma - was not usually spoken of with that phrase.
doubted_claims.problem: Contradicted by the source the answer itself relies on. In 1 Apology 61 Justin connects baptism directly to 'Unless you are born again you will not enter the kingdom of heaven' and calls the rite anagennesis (regeneration). The sentences that follow ('Then came the water. Then came the table.') are incoherent.

doubted_claims.claim: The one who walked with Jesus said it first: a person must be born of water and Spirit.
doubted_claims.problem: States a contested question as settled. That the Fourth Gospel was written by an eyewitness disciple is disputed. Justin's wording ('born again') does not clearly quote John 3:5 and may rest on independent tradition. Whether John was read in worship in every community before 170 is also uncertain.
doubted_claims.source: John 3:3-5; Justin, 1 Apology 61.4; C. E. Hill, The Johannine Corpus in the Early Church (2004)

doubted_claims.claim: a letter written for the emperor and the Senate
doubted_claims.problem: Minor. It is an apology addressed to Antoninus Pius, his sons, the Senate and the Roman people, not a letter.

f4-t-probe-01.reader_note: A lay reader would be confused: the middle paragraph contradicts itself and the quotation does not fit. It needs rewriting.

doubted_claims.claim: First Clement wrote that we are justified not by our own wisdom or works, but by the faith ... God forbid
doubted_claims.problem: Accurate.

doubted_claims.claim: Polycarp wrote that you are saved by grace, not by works, but by the will of God through Jesus Christ
doubted_claims.problem: Accurate (quoting Ephesians 2:8-9).

doubted_claims.claim: Whether an infant carried guilt from birth before any choice was made - our own texts do not say.
doubted_claims.problem: Slightly overstated. Justin contrasts our first birth, 'without our knowledge or choice' and into bad habits, with baptismal rebirth by choice, and speaks of the human race falling under death from Adam. Hermas uses infants as the image of innocence. None of this is a doctrine of inherited guilt, but the texts do touch the question, and the answer should say so.

f1-t-probe-01.reader_note: Clear and the right length. It is a sensible refusal of an anachronistic frame.

doubted_claims.claim: No grave or building from our own time can be shown to be ours.
doubted_claims.problem: Broadly right for buildings and catacombs (the Roman Christian catacomb areas date from c. 200 onward). It should be hedged for the aedicula in the Vatican necropolis (c. 160-170), widely though not universally taken as a Christian memorial and probably the 'trophy' Gaius mentions.
doubted_claims.source: Eusebius, HE 2.25.7 (Gaius); J. Toynbee and J. Ward-Perkins, The Shrine of St Peter (1956)

doubted_claims.claim: He meant it as mockery. It still shows we were visible enough to be mocked
doubted_claims.problem: Pliny's letter is an administrative inquiry, not mockery. The summary of worship is the apostates' exculpatory account. He also reports that the meal had stopped after his edict banning associations, which shows Christians did adjust under pressure. The inference to 'visible' should rest on the denunciations and the anonymous list of names instead.

doubted_claims.claim: We met in houses.
doubted_claims.problem: Fair. Justin, for example, says he lived and taught 'above the baths of Myrtinus'.

f3-e-probe-01.reader_note: Clear and short. It corrects the myth well, apart from the 'mockery' line.

doubted_claims.claim: Whether every household actually sought that approval, we do not know.
doubted_claims.problem: There is no antecedent for 'that approval'. Text seems to have dropped out, and the sentence does not make sense as it stands.

doubted_claims.claim: Nothing in our own record answers that question directly.
doubted_claims.problem: Defensible, since the asker is unknown, but evasive. The sources say a great deal about how outsiders were to be treated: love and pray for enemies, give to everyone who asks, welcome travellers for up to two or three days, and pray for persecutors. The answer could offer that without presuming who the asker is.
doubted_claims.source: Didache 1.3-5, 12.1-2; Justin, 1 Apology 14-15; Epistle to Diognetus 5-6

doubted_claims.claim: most of us could not read or write
doubted_claims.problem: Reasonable and in line with standard estimates of ancient literacy.
doubted_claims.source: W. V. Harris, Ancient Literacy (1989); H. Gamble, Books and Readers in the Early Church (1995)

f6-p-probe-01.reader_note: Understandable but thin, and the broken sentence will puzzle readers. A little more substance from the sources would serve better than the repeated disclaimers.
